title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
summary: Google search alternative Kagi launches a privacy-focused Gmail rival featuring AI capabilities
detailed: Kagi launched a Gmail-like email and calendar service in public beta, emphasizing privacy, customization, and keyboard commands.
The service offers 50GB of storage, unlimited aliases, Sieve filtering, an MCP server, and optional off-by-default AI features for $25 per month via the Kagi Ultimate subscription.
Palo Alto-based software company Kagi is involved in launching the service as a paid alternative to Google.
It provides an ad-free user experience and data sovereignty to compete with major email providers despite lacking native apps and a contacts address book at launch.
sentences: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service.
Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service.
Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist.
Some major features are still missing, though.
As noted, there are no native apps yet.
Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service.
It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan.
It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product.
To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.
Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives.
On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago.
A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.
The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail.

That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)
Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail.
The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now.
There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.
Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail.
Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.
